claims.text: The candidate material is a nanoscale platinum-group-metal high-entropy-alloy or alloy nanoparticle.
The initial catalyst has standard coordination and oxidation-state distributions.
Controlled potential cycling or equivalent stress induces surface restructuring of the catalyst.
Potential-induced restructuring forms low-coordinated PGM sites.
Potential-induced restructuring creates defect sites such as oxygen vacancies.
The restructured sites modify the local electronic structure, including the d-band center.
The catalyst contains a heterogeneous ensemble of sites with varied local electronic structures.
Within the proposed active ensemble, one site adsorbs ethanol.
Sites adjacent to the ethanol-adsorption site facilitate dehydrogenation and oxidation of intermediates.
Dual-site cooperation lowers the energetic barriers for complete 12-electron and 12-proton ethanol oxidation.
The cooperative active-site ensemble suppresses the accumulation of poisoning species such as CO.
Dynamic surface restructuring governs the unusually high ethanol-oxidation activity.
Dynamic surface restructuring governs the unusually high ethanol-oxidation selectivity.
Dynamic surface restructuring and reduced poisoning govern the catalyst's durability during ethanol oxidation.
Relative to steady-potential operation, potential cycling will lower the onset potential for ethanol oxidation.
Relative to steady-potential operation, potential cycling will increase ethanol-oxidation current density.
Potential cycling will increase spectroscopic signatures of low-coordination sites and decrease signals from poisoning intermediates.
Potential cycling will improve long-term durability relative to steady-potential operation.
The restructuring mechanism should dominate at moderate potentials and ambient temperature in aqueous electrolytes.
At very high potentials, extreme pH, or under non-aqueous conditions, restructuring may be suppressed or alternative deactivation pathways may dominate.
